prompt: In a social network, anyone can be friends with anyone.
tells: anyone can be friends with anyone
why: Anyone can link to anyone, so there's no single top and no fixed shape. Items joined by links in any pattern form a graph.
trap: There's no single root or parent.

prompt: A map shows cities joined by roads, and you want the shortest route.
why: Cities are points and roads are connections between them, with many possible routes. Shortest-route problems run on a graph.
trap: A heap may help the search, but the data is a graph.

prompt: In course prerequisites, some classes require several others first.
why: A class can need several others, so an item can have more than one parent. A tree allows only one parent each, so this is a graph.
trap: A tree allows only one parent.

prompt: Web pages link to each other, sometimes in circles.
why: Pages can link back around to where you started, forming loops. Trees never loop, so links with cycles are a graph.

prompt: Flights connect many airports, with several ways to get between two cities.
tells: several ways to get between two cities
why: There are several ways to get between two cities, so paths can split and rejoin. Many routes between the same points means a graph.
trap: A tree has exactly one path.

prompt: A recommendation system links people to products they bought, and products to similar products.
why: People link to products and products link to other products, with no hierarchy. A web of relationships between things is a graph.
trap: Lookups alone don't capture the links between links.
